content.title: Boston Marathon 2026 Results, Prize Money for Korir, Lokedi
content.text: John Korir of Kenya ran the fastest Boston Marathon in history on Monday, breaking the winner’s tape in 2:01:52 to destroy the course record dating back to 2011 at the major marathon. Korir will take home $200,000 from the Boston Athletic Association, the host of the oldest continually run marathon in the U.S., including the $150,000 purse for champions plus a $50,000 bonus for breaking the course record. Both Korir and fellow Kenyan Sharon Lokedi repeated as Boston Marathon champions this year, becoming the first men’s and women’s back-to-back champions at the race since 1995. Lokedi broke the tape in 2:18:51, a bit slower than the 2:17:22 course record she set at last year’s race. In a commercial first, Lokedi completed the race in a pair of signature shoes, the Sharon Lokedi Velociti Elite 3, the first time an Under Armour athlete has competed a major marathon in a signature shoe. Meanwhile, Zouhair Talbi of the U.S. placed fifth in 2:03:45, the fastest time ever recorded by an American man. (Finish times at the Boston Marathon are not eligible for American or world records in part because the course is run at a net downhill.) Jess McClain, the top U.S. woman, also finished in fifth place, running 2:20:49. They will each take home $18,000 in prize money. The top 10 men’s and women’s finishers at the Boston Marathon will all earn prize money, along with the top 10 wheelchair division finishers and the top three masters runners. Wheelchair champions take home $50,000, while the fastest runners over age 40 earn $5,000 checks. The total prize purse for the complete Boston Marathon field is nearly $1.3 million, including course record bonuses. Fastest Qualifying Field Ever The roughly 30,000 runners who participated in Monday’s Boston Marathon will be the fastest field ever assembled for the storied race, thanks to dizzying new qualifying standards in place for the 130th edition. The Boston Marathon is unique among major marathons for requiring the vast majority of its participants to have run a prior 26.2-mile race under a specific time threshold. Given the increasing popularity of running marathons, coupled with tweaks over the past decade to how the Boston Athletic Association has carried out registration for the race, those standards are now faster than ever. Men in the 18-34 age bracket seeking to run the 2026 Boston Marathon were required to have run a previous marathon in 2 hours, 55 minutes or less—the first time the standard in the youngest age group was under three hours. Women and nonbinary individuals in the same age group were required to have run a marathon in under 3 hours, 25 minutes. Applicants must have run the qualifying races between September 2024 and September 2025. Because the volume of applications far exceeded the capped field size for the race, the BAA accepts the fastest qualifiers first—which means even if runners run a Boston Marathon-qualifying time, they may not be accepted into the race. Accepted entries for the 2026 Boston Marathon beat their age group qualifying times by 4 minutes, 35 seconds or more. Nearly 9,000 applications from individuals who had met the Boston Marathon standard for their age group by less than that margin were rejected. In 2025, when the qualifying standard was 3 hours for men and 3 hours, 30 minutes for women and nonbinary individuals in the youngest age bracket, the BAA was forced to reject more than 12,000 qualified applicants, the most ever, and the cut-off time for qualifiers was 6 minutes, 51 seconds. (This story and headline have been updated with the results of the 2026 Boston Marathon. A post-race version of this story has been corrected with the date of the broken course record.)
